podcast.title: Band Name from Gay Subculture
podcast.body: The Toronto group's very name, "Rough Trade," was a term originating from gay subculture, indicating a direct connection to the community and setting a tone for their provocative content. "a Toronto group whose very name was a term from gay subculture."

podcast.title: Emergence as Serious Stars
podcast.body: Rough Trade emerged as one of the serious stars through the late 1970s and into the 1980s, benefiting from the new industry infrastructure and increased radio support for Canadian talent. This period marked a shift towards greater national and international success for homegrown artists. "Love her boy, Chilla Wack, Bruce Coburn, rough trade, the pay-all was Toronto, the headpins, the spoons, bride-adams, parachute club, men without hats, Cory Hart. They all emerged as serious stars through the late 1970s and into the 1980s."

podcast.title: True North Records Success
podcast.body: Rough Trade was among the artists on Bernie Finkelstein's True North Records who achieved "legitimate hits" due to the support provided by Cancon quotas. "True North was unabashedly Canadian, and thanks to the Cancon quotas, a few of their acts broke through and had legitimate hits, artists like Bruce Cobard in Rough Trade."

xref.title: First Openly Gay Alt-Rock Role Model (Canadian)
xref.body: Carol Pope is identified as one of the first openly gay alt-rock role models in the world, and notably, she was Canadian. She fronted the Toronto group Rough Trade. "One of the first openly gay, alt-rock role models in the world was a woman and a Canadian."

srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Formation at Bristol University
xref.body: The English alt-rock band The Sundays formed after singer Harriet Wheeler and guitarist David Gavurin met while attending Bristol University in the late 1980s. They began dating, formed a band, and secured a deal with Rough Trade Records. "They met when singer Harriet Wheeler met guitarist David Gavarin while they were attending Bristol University in the middle ladies. They started dating, then a band was assembled, and they got a deal with rough trade records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Couples in Music

xref.title: Founding Mute Records
xref.body: Using the profits from "Warm Leatherette," Daniel Miller established his own independent record label, Mute, dedicated exclusively to guitar-less music, which later introduced artists like Depeche Mode, Erasure, and Yazoo. "He took the profits and founded his own independent record label devoted entirely to guitar less music. He called the label Mute."

xref.title: North American Label Indifference & UK Interest
xref.body: Initially, no US labels expressed interest in releasing their material, prompting the band to send a demo to Rough Trade Records in the UK, which then agreed to release their *The Modern Age* EP. "Nobody in the US was interested in releasing their stuff, so they sent a demo to rough trade records in the UK, who agreed to release an EP called The Modern Age."

xref.title: Problems with Rough Trade Records
xref.body: The band experienced significant problems with their record company, Rough Trade, which worsened after "The Queen Is Dead" was released. These issues were so prominent that they were even satirized in the song "Frankly, Mr. Shankly." "The problems with rough trade got worse."

xref.title: Rock's First Openly Gay Rock Star
xref.body: Little Richard is argued to be rock's first openly gay rock star, or at least bisexual with strong gay leanings. He openly embraced effeminate mannerisms, wore makeup, engaged in "rough trade," and famously declared, "Elvis may have been the king of rock and roll, but I and the queen." "you can make an argument that he was Rock's first openly gay rock star."

xref.title: Signed by UK Label After US Rejection
xref.body: Despite generating buzz, The Strokes initially failed to secure interest from any American record labels. They subsequently sent demos to Rough Trade in the UK, which signed them after "loved what they heard." "Interestingly, despite the buzz, the Strokes could not interest any American labels in what they were doing. So they sent some demos to Rough Trade in the UK, and Rough Trade loved what they heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: The Modern Age EP and Bidding War
xref.body: The Strokes recorded a three-track demo in 2000, which was unusually tight for a young group due to their insistence on rehearsing to a click track. This led to "The Modern Age" EP, which sold well and ignited one of the fiercest bidding wars among record labels in a long time. Rough Trade Records (UK) won the bid, prompting label head Geoff Travis to resurrect the label to sign The Strokes. They also secured a deal with RCA, which was amenable to the band's desire to make a music video. "The subsequent EP, the three track, the modern age, not only sold respectively well, but also sparked a bidding war amongst record labels."
